q: Does CUDA++ need libcuda?
alt: Can CUDA++ run without the CUDA driver library?
Is libcuda loaded by CUDA++?
a: No. Drake replaced `libcuda` with his own client for the open kernel module's ioctls (`nvrm/nvrm.c` and `m16/`). The library links no CUDA library. The one exception in the tree is `tools/interop/cubin_probe`, a separate tool that links `libcuda` on purpose to test whether NVIDIA's driver accepts a cubin CUDA++ exported. Lesson 1 shows the grep.

q: What NVIDIA software does CUDA++ still depend on?
alt: What parts of NVIDIA's stack remain under CUDA++?
Is CUDA++ completely free of NVIDIA software?
a: Two things below the user-space line: NVIDIA's open kernel module (`nvidia.ko`, `nvidia-uvm.ko`, exactly version 580.173.02) and the GSP firmware inside the GPU, which the chip signature-checks. Aien's own GB10 driver to replace the modules is BUILDING on the roadmap; the firmware stays NVIDIA's.

q: Which device files does a CUDA program use on Linux?
alt: What does libcuda open under /dev?
How does user space talk to the NVIDIA kernel module?
a: Three: `/dev/nvidiactl` for the resource manager (alloc, control, free), `/dev/nvidia<minor>` (e.g. `/dev/nvidia0`) for CPU mappings, and `/dev/nvidia-uvm` for the unified-memory driver that owns the GPU page tables. Everything goes through `ioctl` and `mmap` on those.

q: Has CUDA++ been qualified on the GB10?
alt: Is the CUDA++ native GPU path proven on hardware right now?
Does CUDA++ pass on the chip?
a: At the pinned commit, CUDApp's own README says current native qualification is **NOT_RUN**. The older M16 receipt is kept as an unauditable historical summary because its raw logs are absent. Historical chip receipts exist (for example the 2026-10-13 tensor-core ceiling run), but they qualify their own dates and commits, not this checkout.

q: Where does the NVIDIA RM API live in the open kernel module?
alt: Which headers define the resource manager interface?
Where are NV_ESC codes defined?
a: Escape codes: `nv_escape.h` (RM ops) and `nv-ioctl-numbers.h` (device ops). Parameter structs: `nvos.h`. Object classes: `class/clXXXX.h`, one header per class number. Control commands: `ctrl/`. UVM calls: `kernel-open/nvidia-uvm/uvm_ioctl.h`. Drake vendors the 67 he needs, unchanged, in `third_party/nvidia-open-580.173.02/`.

q: What is a class id in the NVIDIA driver?
alt: What does a class number like 0x2080 mean?
What is BLACKWELL_COMPUTE_B?
a: It says what kind of object you are creating with `NV_ESC_RM_ALLOC`. 0x2080 is `NV20_SUBDEVICE_0` (header `class/cl2080.h`), 0xC96F is `BLACKWELL_CHANNEL_GPFIFO_A`, 0xCEC0 is `BLACKWELL_COMPUTE_B`. The escape code says which operation; the class says which kind of object.

q: How is an RM control command number built?
alt: What do the bits of NV2080_CTRL_CMD_GR_GET_INFO mean?
How do I decode a control command id?
a: Per `ctrl/ctrlxxxx.h`: CLASS in bits 31..16, CATEGORY in 13..8, INDEX in 7..0. So 0x20801201 is subdevice class 0x2080, category 0x12 (graphics), index 1. The class part tells you which object to send it to. Lesson 2's `ctrl.om` splits them and refuses a number with the unused bits 14..15 set.

q: Are UVM ioctl numbers encoded like the NVIDIA control ioctls?
alt: Why do UVM ioctls look like small plain numbers?
Does UVM_INITIALIZE use _IOC?
a: No. On Linux `UVM_IOCTL_BASE(i)` is just `i`, so UVM requests carry no size. The payload size lives only in the header's structs, which is why omega-mv's `uvmctl` word keeps an explicit allowlist of request and size pairs for ABI 580.173.02.

q: How is an NVIDIA ioctl request number computed?
alt: What is 0xc020462b?
How do I build NV_ESC_RM_ALLOC's ioctl number?
a: It is Linux `_IOC(dir, type, nr, size)`: direction 3 (read and write) in bits 31..30, `sizeof` the parameter struct in 29..16, `'F'` in 15..8, the escape in 7..0. For `NV_ESC_RM_ALLOC` (0x2B) with the 32-byte `NVOS21_PARAMETERS` that is 0xc020462b. Lesson 3 computes it in Omega and finds the same literal in CUDApp's `context.om`.

q: Why is the card info ioctl size 4608?
alt: How big is nv_ioctl_card_info_t?
Why does struct padding matter for ioctls?
a: `nv_ioctl_card_info_t` is 72 bytes once C alignment padding is included (a 1-byte flag before a 4-byte-aligned PCI struct, then 8-byte-aligned 64-bit fields), and CUDApp asks for 64 cards: 4608. Summing the fields gives 65 bytes and a request number nothing uses. The example shows both.

q: How does Omega issue an ioctl?
alt: What is devctl in Omega?
Can Omega call NVIDIA ioctls?
a: The pinned compiler has checked device words (ids 166 to 177). `devctl fd request A off n` takes a literal request; at compile time `omc` accepts only FIONREAD or a read/write `'F'` request with a non-zero size (a write-only one is error 9), and at run time the span must equal the encoded size (else trap 3, exit 103). GPU launch through these words is not qualified.

q: In what order are GPU objects created?
alt: What is the RM object tree for a compute channel?
What does nvrm_open allocate?
a: In CUDApp: root client, then device; subdevice and virtual memory under the device; the usermode (doorbell) page under the subdevice; the address space and memory under the device; then a channel group, a context share and the GPFIFO channel under the group, and the Blackwell compute object under the channel. Lesson 4 replays that order in an Omega model.

q: What is an RM handle?
alt: Who picks object handles in the NVIDIA driver?
What is hObjectNew?
a: A 32-bit name for an object, used in later calls. In CUDApp's `rm_alloc` the client picks it from a counter and passes it as `hObjectNew`; only the root client is allocated with 0 and gets its handle back from the driver.

q: What happens to child objects when I free a parent?
alt: Does freeing the root client free everything?
Can I use a channel after freeing its channel group?
a: Freeing an object frees its whole subtree, and freeing the root client frees everything. A handle to a child of a freed parent is no longer an object. In Drake's model, freeing the channel group removes four objects and a later allocation under the old channel is refused.

q: Why does creating the compute object sometimes fail with NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY?
alt: Why does CUDApp retry the compute class allocation?
What is NVRM_CHANNEL_NO_MEMORY_RETRIES?
a: That allocation needs one free, physically contiguous 2 MiB block of host memory for the channel's context buffer, which can be briefly missing on a busy host. CUDApp retries that one error, 50 times at 100 ms, and treats every other error as final.

q: How does work get submitted to an NVIDIA GPU without a system call?
alt: What is a doorbell?
How does nvrm_ring work?
a: The CPU writes a pushbuffer, writes one 8-byte GPFIFO ring entry pointing at it, advances `GPPut` in the USERD page with a barrier on each side, then rings the doorbell: one 32-bit store of the channel's work-submit token into the usermode page. No system call is made.

q: What is the layout of a GPFIFO entry?
alt: How is a GPFIFO entry encoded on Blackwell?
What are GP_ENTRY0 and GP_ENTRY1?
a: Per `clc96f.h`: `GP_ENTRY0_GET` (31:2) holds the low address bits, `GP_ENTRY1_GET_HI` (7:0) the high ones, `GP_ENTRY1_LENGTH` (30:10) the length in 32-bit words, plus `LEVEL` (9:9) and `SYNC` (31:31). Lesson 5 builds one and decodes it back.

q: What is a pushbuffer method header?
alt: How does nvrm_mthd encode a method?
Why is the method offset shifted right by 2?
a: CUDApp writes it as 2 in the top bits (incrementing), the data count from bit 16, the subchannel from bit 13 and the method offset in dwords in the low bits. Headers list offsets in bytes (`SEM_ADDR_LO` is 0x5c), so the encoder stores 0x5c >> 2. Forgetting the shift selects a different method.

q: What is a QMD?
alt: What is the compute launch descriptor on Blackwell?
How does CUDA++ launch a kernel?
a: The QMD is the launch descriptor: 96 words (384 bytes) with grid and block size, registers, shared memory, code address and constant buffer. CUDA++ builds it in `src/omega_blackwell_qmd.c` and hands its address, shifted right by 8, to the compute class with `SEND_PCAS_A` in `src/omega_gpu_cmdlist.c`; layout facts are cited to Mesa's `nak/qmd.rs`.

q: Is GPFIFO LEVEL set to MAIN in CUDApp?
alt: What does bit 41 of nvrm_gp_entry mean?
Is there a mismatch in nvrm_gp_entry's comment?
a: The code sets bit 41, which is `GP_ENTRY1_LEVEL`, to 1, and `clc96f.h` names value 1 `SUBROUTINE` (MAIN is 0). The comment above `nvrm_gp_entry` says MAIN. So the comment and the code disagree at this pin; the code is what the historical chip runs used, and MAIN has not been tried.

q: Is a host test run the same as hardware qualification?
alt: Does make test prove CUDA++ works on the GPU?
Is the simulator a qualification?
a: No. Host tests and simulators prove the code agrees with Drake's model of the chip. Qualification is a chip gate on a named commit with a receipt and its raw logs. Lesson 6 keeps host results, historical chip results and current qualification in separate sentences.

q: How can I check a CUDApp receipt without a GPU?
alt: How do I verify a receipt's SHA256SUMS?
What does INCOMPLETE mean for a receipt?
a: Re-hash every file the receipt lists. All match: PASS for integrity only. A file missing: INCOMPLETE, find out why. A hash differs: FAIL. Nothing checked: NOT_RUN, never PASS. Then confirm the commit and that raw logs exist. Lesson 6's `verdict.om` does exactly this.

q: What did the M16 gate prove?
alt: What is m16_requalify?
How do you prove a GPU ran your command and not something else?
a: It queued a semaphore release without ringing the doorbell and checked the marker stayed 0 for 100 ms, rang it and checked the marker became 0x16c0ffee, and read `/proc/self/maps` to prove `libcuda` was never loaded. Its receipt at this pin is an unauditable historical summary because the raw logs are absent.

q: What is a mutation test in CUDApp?
alt: Why must a deliberately broken copy fail?
What does gpu_engine_mutations.sh do?
a: It copies the engine to a scratch directory, breaks one protection at a time, rebuilds the test and requires it to fail. A mutant that is not caught fails the sweep. A check that cannot fail proves nothing.

q: Did CUDA++ use NVIDIA source code?
alt: Is NVIDIA code in CUDApp?
Which NVIDIA files does CUDA++ include?
a: Only 67 header files from NVIDIA's open-gpu-kernel-modules 580.173.02, MIT, copied unchanged with their notices (60 with an SPDX MIT line, 7 with the MIT text only). They are used as user-space interface definitions; no kernel module is built from them. No libcuda, firmware or PTX is shipped.

q: Did Drake disassemble NVIDIA binaries?
alt: Was libcuda reverse engineered?
How was the GPU instruction encoding learned legally?
a: Per `docs/HOW_I_DID_IT.md`: he did not take apart `libcuda`, `nvcc` or any other NVIDIA program. He compiled small probe kernels of his own with NVIDIA's compiler, printed them with NVIDIA's disassembler, compared them, cross-checked with Mesa's MIT-licensed NAK, and confirmed on the chip. This is a description of method, not legal advice.

q: Did CUDA++ copy code from Mesa?
alt: How is Mesa used in CUDA++?
Is NVK code in CUDApp?
a: `THIRD_PARTY.md` says Mesa NVK/NAK (MIT) is cited in comments as the source of hardware facts (opcode bits, latencies, the QMD layout, the dispatch order), the encoder, scheduler and command-list code is Drake's own, and the latency values in one file were taken from Mesa's tables, with the notices reproduced.

q: What licence is CUDApp under?
alt: Can I reuse CUDA++ code?
Is CUDA++ Apache or MIT?
a: At the pin the first-party `LICENSE` is Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, and an earlier MIT snapshot is preserved. NVIDIA's headers keep MIT. Some files, including the native `.om` sources under `native/`, carry an `AGPL-3.0-only` SPDX line, so check the header of the exact file you reuse.

q: What does a GB10 machine instruction look like?
alt: How big is an sm_121 instruction?
What is SASS on Blackwell?
a: 128 bits, stored as four little-endian 32-bit words. Word 0 has the opcode (bits 0..11), predicate (12..15), destination (16..23) and first source (24..31); words 1 and 2 hold more operands and modifiers; word 3 is the scheduling control word. Register 255 is RZ.

q: What are stall counts and scoreboards in SASS?
alt: What is the control word of a GPU instruction?
How does the GPU know to wait for a load?
a: In word 3: stall in bits 9..12, yield 13, write scoreboard 14..16, read scoreboard 17..19, wait mask 20..25 (7 in a scoreboard field means none). Slow instructions set a scoreboard; later ones wait on it. In the seed vector add both loads set SB4 and the add waits on SB4 with a 5-cycle stall.

q: How did Drake learn the undocumented GPU instruction encoding?
alt: How do you reverse engineer SASS?
Where did the sm_121 encodings come from?
a: Three sources, all checked on the chip: his own probe kernels compiled once with `nvcc` and printed with `cuobjdump` (change one detail, see which bits move), Mesa's open NAK compiler (cited, not copied), and the GB10 itself, where an encoding is believed only when it gives the right answer.

q: Does CUDA++ have its own disassembler?
alt: Is nvdisasm still needed?
What is roadmap bar C6?
a: Not yet in CUDApp. Bar C6 is BUILDING on an Omega branch, and some CUDApp host tests still call NVIDIA's `nvdisasm` as an optional cross-check when it is installed. Lesson 8's decoder reads fields; it is not a full disassembler.
